en: I bow my head to that King Kulaśekhara, in whose city the festival of the theater is proclaimed day after day.
O Mukunda, make me one who daily addresses You as "Śrīvallabha," "Varada," "Dayāpara," "Bhaktapriya," "Bhavaluṇṭhanakovida," "Nātha," "Nāgaśayana," and "Jagannivāsa."

Victory, victory to this god, the delight of Devakī! Victory, victory to Kṛṣṇa, the lamp of the Vṛṣṇi lineage! Victory, victory to him who is dark as a cloud, whose limbs are tender! Victory, victory to Mukunda, the destroyer of the earth’s burden! KMukm_2 //
Having prostrated with my head before Mukunda, I entreat you for this one singular request:
by your grace, may there be no forgetting of your lotus feet in birth after birth.
O Hari, I do not worship the pair of your feet for the sake of freedom from duality, nor to remove even the heavy hellish torment of Kumbhīpāka;
nor to sport with lovely women of tender limbs in the Nandana grove. In every state of being, within the temple of my heart, I shall meditate upon you alone.

I have no attachment to the Dharma, nor to the accumulation of wealth, nor indeed to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; whatever is destined to happen, let it be so, O Blessed One, in accordance with my past karma.
This alone is my earnest prayer and great desire: may unwavering devotion toward the pair of your lotus feet remain with me, even in birth after birth.
O Destroyer of Hell, let my dwelling be as I desire in heaven, on earth, or even in hell;
yet at the moment of death, I shall think only of Your feet, which have cast aside the autumnal lotuses.
O Kṛṣṇa, let the royal swan of my mind enter the interior of the cage of your lotus feet this very day;
for when the time comes for the departure of life, and the throat is obstructed by phlegm, wind, and bile, how could there be remembrance of you?
I constantly meditate upon Hari alone— the son of Nanda the cowherd, who is higher than the highest, whose lotus-face bears a gentle, slow smile,
and who is worshipped by the multitude of sages beginning with Nārada.

Having plunged into the lake of Hari— whose lotus-feet and fish-like eyes are radiant, which dispels fatigue, and whose unfathomable depths are agitated by the waves of his arms— I drink in the flood of its splendor-water and, exhausted by the desert of worldly existence, cast off my weariness today.
O mind, do not desist from sporting with the slayer of Mura, whose eyes are like lotuses and who holds the conch and discus;
I know of no other bliss that is ever equal to the nectar of remembering the feet of Hari.
Do not fear, O slow-witted one; reflect deeply. These long-lasting torments do not prevail over us, for our Lord is indeed Śrīdhara.
Cast off indolence and meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, who is easily attained through devotion. Is He, the remover of the world's calamities, not capable of helping His servant?
For those who have entered the ocean of existence, struck by the winds of dualities, oppressed by the burden of protecting sons, daughters, and wives,
and sinking without a raft in the turbulent waters of the sense-objects— may the single boat of Viṣṇu be the refuge for men.

"Do not let your mind fall into despondency, thinking, 'How shall I cross this bottomless and difficult-to-traverse ocean of existence? Your singular devotion, fixed upon the lotus-eyed Lord who destroys the hells, will certainly carry you across."

O Giver of Boons, O Abode of the Three, grant us the boat of devotion to Your lotus feet for those of us sinking in the great ocean called saṃsāra— an ocean where craving is the water, delusion is the series of waves tossed by the wind of passion, and the whirlpool is the wife, crowded with the swarms of crocodiles that are sons and kin.

May I not see, even for a moment, those whose merit is exhausted and who are devoid of devotion at Your lotus feet; may I not hear Your narrable life-story, having cast aside all other collections of tales;
O Mādhava, Lord of the World, may I never remember You with a mind that denies You; and may I never be deprived of the practice of Your worship, even in birth after birth.

O tongue, proclaim Keśava, the enemy of Mura; O mind, take refuge in Śrīdhara; O pair of hands, worship the stories of Acyuta; O pair of ears, listen! O pair of eyes, behold Kṛṣṇa; O feet, go to the abode of Hari; O sense of smell, scent the *tulasī* from the feet of Mukunda; O head, bow down to Adhokṣaja! KMukm_16 //
O people, listen! Those sages who know yoga, such as Yājñavalkya and others, proclaim this remedy for birth, death, and disease:
let the immeasurable, singular, immortal light within, called Kṛṣṇa, be drunk; when that supreme medicine is drunk, it bestows ultimate liberation.

O mortals, listen to that which is for your supreme benefit; I shall speak it to you in brief. Having properly entered this ocean of saṃsāra, which abounds with the waves of calamity, and having cast aside various forms of ignorance from your minds, you should repeatedly set in motion this mantra—"Namo Nārāyaṇāya"—together with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and accompanied by prostration. 18.

Earth is but a speck of dust, water is but droplets, fire is but a feeble spark, wind is but a faint breath, space is but a minute void, and all the gods, from Rudra and Pitāmaha down to the lowliest, are but insects—before whom that [vision] of yours triumphs upon this earth, reaching its limit only at the state of the shaken-off (the liberated). (KMukm 19)

O Lotus-eyed One, may our lives always be fulfilled for us who constantly savor the nectar of meditating upon the pair of your lotus-feet—with joined palms, with bowed heads, with limbs bristling with horripilation, with throats choked by emotion, and with eyes shedding streams of tears. (KMukm 20)

O Gopālaka! O ocean of compassion! O Lord of the daughter of the ocean! O slayer of Kaṃsa! O you who have crossed to the further shore of mercy for the lordly elephant! O Mādhava! O younger brother of Rāma! O teacher of the three worlds! O lotus-eyed one! O Lord of the cowherd women, protect me; for I know nothing other than You. (KMukm 21)

May the crest-jewel of the cowherds bestow upon us supreme welfare— he who is the emerald for the serpent-like misfortunes of his devotees, the jewel that protects the three worlds, the jewel-cloud for the *cātaka*-birds of the Gopīs’ eyes, the jewel-seal of beauty, the jewel of beloveds, the sole ornament-jewel upon the pair of Rukmiṇī’s firm breasts, and the crown-jewel of the gods.

O tongue, chant, chant incessantly the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the sole mantra for severing enemies, the mantra honored by all the words of the Upaniṣads, the mantra for crossing over saṃsāra, the mantra for the departure from the mass of accumulated darkness, the sole mantra for all sovereignty, the mantra for protection from those bitten by the serpent of calamity, and the mantra that makes birth fruitful.

O mind, drink this divine medicine of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the medicine that pacifies delusion, the medicine for the movement of the sage’s mental faculties, the medicine that removes the suffering of the lords of the Daityas, the sole life-restoring medicine in the three worlds, the medicine most beneficial to devotees, the sole medicine for the total destruction of the fear of worldly existence, and the medicine that brings about the attainment of the highest good.

The study of the sacred scriptures is but a wailing in the wilderness; the daily observances of the Vedas yield only the fruit of cutting away one's fat; all ritual acts of public charity are like offerings poured upon ashes;
and the plunging into sacred fords is like the bathing of an elephant—unless they are accompanied by the remembrance of the two lotus-feet of that Lord Nārāyaṇa, who alone is truly victorious.
Having uttered the glorious name known as Nārāyaṇa, who—even among the sinful—has not attained their desire?
Alas! Our speech did not previously proceed toward it; therefore, we have experienced the sufferings of dwelling in the womb and so forth.
O Enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, this birth is the fruit [of my previous merit]; this very favor of Yours is what I must pray for:
"Remember me, O Lord of the World, as the servant of the servant of the servant of the servant of Your own servant. (KMukm 27)
While our Lord Nārāyaṇa—the Supreme Person, the sole sovereign of the three worlds, the one to be served with the heart, and the giver of his own station—remains present;
yet we search for some lowly man, a mere lord of a few villages who grants but little, for the sake of service—alas, how mute and wretched we are! (KMukm 28)
O Madana, you have become emaciated by the fire of Śiva’s eye while occupying a place in my mind that is the abode of Mukunda’s lotus feet;
do you not remember the prowess of Murāri’s discus?

O tongue, proclaiming the supreme reality beyond all else, which, like honey, distills the fruits of the virtuous—do thou set in motion the names that have Nārāyaṇa as their object; I stand before thee with palms joined in reverence.
This body, delicate by its very nature of transformation, will inevitably fall apart with its joints loosened and decayed;
why do you torment yourself with medicines, O fool of wicked mind? Drink the healthy elixir of Kṛṣṇa!

The ocean is your wife; the son of the best of oysters (Śrī) is your daughter; Viriñca (Brahmā) is your son; the Veda is your hymn of praise; the host of gods is your circle of servants; grace is your favor; liberation is your illusion; and the entire world without exception is yours. Devakī is your mother, and the son of Balaripu (Kṛṣṇa) is your friend; beyond this, I know nothing else of you.

May Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the three worlds, protect us; I bow down to Kṛṣṇa; by Kṛṣṇa the enemies of the immortals were struck down; salutation to that Kṛṣṇa! From Kṛṣṇa alone this entire world has arisen; I am the servant of Kṛṣṇa; all this remains within Kṛṣṇa; O Kṛṣṇa, protect me!
Therefore, be gracious, O Blessed One; show compassion toward me, who am without a protector, O Viṣṇu, for you are indeed supremely compassionate.
O Ananta, O Hari, it behooves you to lift up this wretched one submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, for you are the Supreme Person.
I bow to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa; I always perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa;
I utter the stainless name of Nārāyaṇa; and I remember the imperishable reality of Nārāyaṇa.
O Śrīnātha, Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Śrīkṛṣṇa, beloved of devotees, wielder of the discus; O Śrīpadmanābha, Acyuta, slayer of Kaiṭabha, Śrīrāma, lotus-eyed one, Hari, Murāri! KMukm_36 //
Though capable of uttering "Ananta, Vaikuṇṭha, Mukunda, Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, Dāmodara, Mādhava," no one speaks them; alas, how people are intent upon their own ruin!
Those who meditate upon Viṣṇu— the infinite and imperishable one— constantly established within the center of the heart-lotus,
being ever composed, attain the supreme Vaiṣṇava perfection that bestows eternal fearlessness.
Salutations to Mādhava, the enemy of Madhu, whose beautiful form is starred by the spray from the waves of the milk ocean, and who reclines upon the couch of the serpent’s coils.

This work was composed by King Kulaśekhara, who, like a bee at the lotus-feet of the Lotus-Eyed One, had as his two dear friends two learned and retentive men, heroes among poets and the best of the twice-born, Padma and Śara. KMukm_40.
